extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and early-career professional mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on how to conduct mathematical research, run/participate in seminars, write papers and books, collaborate, and publish so as to build a research career and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily focused practice (four productive hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: My teacher and friend Fred Almgren used to say that a graduate student should spend four hours every day doing mathematics; ... it is nearly impossible to do serious mathematical research for more than four or five hours in a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doing mathematics be uninterrupted and intensely focused (no music, coffee cups, phone calls, email, door interruptions). Go somewhere you cannot be interrupted, sit with paper and pen, think and calculate, try things, make mistakes, learn from them. If you can produce four productive hours like this five or six days per week you will be a very successful mathematician. Note the author’s observation that one cannot productively sustain more than ~4–5 serious research hours a day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require contiguous chunks of time
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have non-trivial, contiguous chunks of time in which to do your work. Doing mathematics is not like polishing shoes—you cannot do your work in 20-minute snatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can take an hour to get ideas organized before real work begins. You need leisure to turn ideas over, try different approaches, attempt to disprove as well as prove. Short snatches (e.g., 20 minutes) are usually not useful; plan for longer uninterrupted blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept failure, learn, and be tenacious
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenacity and self-confidence are two of the most important attributes that you can have. Maintain your modesty and your dignity, but cultivate these two essential properties in yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paper is rejected, read reports carefully, learn from them, show the paper to mentors/peers, improve it, and resubmit. Publishing setbacks (rejections, harsh referee reports) are normal—use them to make the work better and persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have something new to write about
rubrics_metrics.description: It is virtually impossible in mathematics to write a paper (and to get it published!) that says, 'This morning I woke up and tried to prove the Riemann hypothesis and I failed.' ... The necessary and sufficient condition for being able to write a new paper (assuming that this is not an expository paper) is that you have a non-trivial new result to present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only write a research paper when you have a genuine new theorem/result; expository papers are the exception and have different goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and define your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The next pre-requisite for effective writing is that you consider carefully who your audience is. Is it graduate students? Undergraduates? Fully vested mathematicians? Researchers? Specialists in your subject area?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deciding the audience determines how much background and jargon you can assume, how much motivation to provide, and how detailed explanations should be. Tailor abstract/introduction and level of exposition to the intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish the Abstract and Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Your new paper should be well organized. It should begin with an Abstract. ... Most readers will read your abstract, and many readers will read your introduction. The number that will forge on beyond that is rather small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a brief, pithy, eye-catching Abstract and a concise (often one page) introduction that (i) explains what the paper is about, (ii) what background is needed, (iii) what the main result is, and (iv) whether the reader wants to continue. Polish these sections highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present notation and precise statements before proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The next part of the paper could give some notation and statements of key supporting ideas. ... You may follow this section with a section that (building on the material just described) gives careful and rigorous statements of the main theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring the reader up to speed with notation and precise theorem statements before diving into lengthy proofs; this is comforting and standard for mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide proof overviews for long proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proofs that you are going to present are really difficult and tricky, then it is nice to provide a section that outlines the key steps of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give an overview of main steps when full proofs are long/complicated to help the reader navigate the detailed technical argument; omit only when the proof is short and easy to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize proofs with lemmas/propositions and intermediary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do take advantage of the formalism of modern mathematics to help you lay things out. Have enunciated lemmas, propositions, sublemmas, and so forth to organize the ideas and break the reasoning up into steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intermediate statements, remind the reader where they are and what is being proved, let proofs span sections if necessary, and avoid hanging lemmas/unproved claims—make hypotheses explicit and up-front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude with summarizing remarks and future directions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is always a bit nicer, and certainly more effective communication, to have some concluding remarks that draw all your ideas together, point out what has been accomplished and how, and suggest further avenues of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a Concluding Remarks section or similar summary so readers see the accomplishments and potential follow-ups—akin to a good talk ending with summatory observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague global declarations; repeat important hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: It is also good exposition to avoid making universal statements like, 'From now on all spaces are paracompact and semi-metric.' ... It is difficult for the reader to remember such declarations, and certainly not much trouble to repeat them as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer repeating important assumptions where relevant rather than relying on sweeping 'from now on' statements which can confuse readers; repetition aids comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the reader when ending proofs (avoid cryptic endings)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is OK ... to end a paper with something like '... and therefore the sequence converges hemi-semi-demi uniformly at almost every point of the pseudo-set.' ... But such an ending is also quite likely to leave the reader saying, 'Huh??'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concluding remarks that clearly tie up the argument rather than abrupt or opaque final lines—help the reader confirm the proof is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing books is a long, different commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: A monograph can be your definitive statement about your subject area ... A book is a different type of writing, with a different sort of audience, and certainly different goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books take far longer than papers (could take years), involve major organizational decisions, and require planning about scope/content. Discuss plans with colleagues, weigh career impact, and be realistic about the time/work required to finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider career and institutional valuation of books vs papers
rubrics_metrics.description: You should be aware that bookwriting is not necessarily rewarded in the same way that paper writing is. ... Books tend to be exposition, and exposition is valuable. But it is not proving theorems. And your Chair and your Dean know it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how your institution values books versus peer-reviewed papers before committing significant time to a monograph; at some institutions textbooks/monographs are valued more than at research-heavy institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan publisher interactions and time management for books
rubrics_metrics.description: On top of all that, you must gird your loins and figure out how to deal with a publisher. ... You must talk about scheduling, copy editing, royalties, and a variety of other issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to negotiate schedules, editing, royalties, and possibly a web presence; consider using web supplements to keep material current and provide extras (graphics, exercises, animated diagrams) if publisher supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working alone: be aware of risks and potentials
rubrics_metrics.description: The default mode of work in the academic mathematics profession is to labor away on your own. ... It is a tough life to cut out for yourself, with potential big wins and possibly catastrophic losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solo work offers flexibility and ownership over discoveries but risks discouragement, isolation, or personal costs; cultivate the ability to salvage partial progress into publishable insights rather than discarding everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mathematics as participatory even if you work solo
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you don’t collaborate, you should treat mathematics as a participatory endeavor. Talk to people. Go to seminars. Attend conferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with seminars, conferences, publish papers, and socialize ideas; participation keeps you focused, provides reality checks, and helps progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration etiquette: pitch in and volunteer tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually the question of who will do what, and who will contribute what, is answered automatically as the ideas develop. Everyone should really want to be part of this team. Everyone should really want to pitch in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tasks arise collaborators should volunteer (e.g., 'I’ll write a draft' or 'Let me try that calculation'). Avoid shirking and be willing to do needed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship norms and avoid credit disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom (unlike in other sciences) is to list the authors alphabetically. So there should be no squabbling over priorities or ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept alphabetical authorship as standard; do not obsess over relative contributions on individual papers—collaboration returns vary across projects and future papers may invert apparent contribution levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide moral support and appreciate coauthors
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of your job as a collaborator is to provide moral support (and praise, when appropriate) for your co-workers. Some of the work will be difficult and confusing, other parts will be long and tedious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage teammates, explain ideas to them, say kind words when someone contributes, and lend a hand where appropriate—this fosters a healthy collaborative environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect collaborators’ differing strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone brings something different to the altar. Some are good at concepts, others at calculation. Some shine at writing the stuff up, others at posing the critical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value complementary skills (conceptual, computational, expository) and assign tasks to match strengths; mutual respect improves outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose collaborators carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: You want to exercise some care in choosing your collaborators. There is one guy in my field who has a universal reputation as a rapscallion, a thief, a charlatan, and a misanthrope. I won’t even talk to him, much less collaborate with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer collaborators you like, share interests/goals with, and trust. Avoid those with reputations for unprofessional behavior; good choices lead to many happy team efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use preprint servers but value peer-reviewed journals
rubrics_metrics.description: It is quite simple to post [your paper] on the Internet. For mathematicians these days the canonical place to put your paper is the preprint server arXiv. ... But Seiberg and Witten ultimately published their ideas in a standard venue (the Journal of High Energy Physics)—that is to say, a recognized, refereed, scholarly journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post preprints (arXiv) to disseminate results quickly and invite discussion, but also pursue peer-reviewed publication because refereeing is validation, and refereed journals are what counts for tenure, promotion, and formal recognition.
